y9-0: Blocking blood vessels for knee osteoarthritis: promising, but the evidence is still weak
y9-1: In a study published in Radiology by researchers at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin in Germany, genicular artery embolisation was performed in 194 people with knee osteoarthritis (median age 69) whose knee pain persisted despite at least 3 months of physiotherapy, medication and injections. In this procedure, microspheres that dissolve within a few hours are delivered through a thin catheter into the small blood vessels supplying the knee, temporarily reducing blood flow in those vessels. On a 0–10 scale, median pain fell from 7 to 3 at 12 months; 80% of those who completed the assessment improved meaningfully. There were no serious side effects; mild, temporary problems occurred in 6.7% of procedures.
y9-2: This study had no comparison group, so a placebo effect and pain easing naturally over time cannot be ruled out. In a 58-patient study comparing the procedure with a sham, there was no significant difference between the groups at 12 months, and an analysis combining three randomised trials also found no advantage over a sham procedure. The method does not repair cartilage, and it is not known whether it delays joint replacement. Larger, controlled studies are needed.
y9-3: Sources: ScienceDaily (RSNA), 14 October 2026 · Radiology, 2026
y9-4: Robotic knee and hip replacement was no better than conventional surgery in the early years
y9-6: In two studies published in The BMJ, researchers from Queen Mary University of London and the universities of Oxford and Bristol analysed 2018–2024 data from the National Joint Registry for England and Wales: 666,283 hip replacements (10,203 robot-assisted) and 697,145 knee replacements (22,111 robot-assisted). Over an average follow-up of 2.5 years, there was no difference between robot-assisted and conventional surgery in implant survival or the risk of repeat surgery (revision). In the hip, robot-assisted surgery was linked to a lower risk of revisions possibly related to implant malpositioning, but this did not reduce the overall revision risk. Patient survival after hip replacement did not differ either.
y9-7: This is an observational study: it used a method designed to mimic a randomised trial, but unmeasured differences may have affected the results. Follow-up was short; long-term differences and patient outcomes such as pain and daily function have not yet been compared, and ongoing randomised trials will show these. Robotic systems cost around £1 million to install and add £1,000–2,500 to each operation.
y9-8: Sources: BMJ Group, 30 September 2026 · The BMJ, 2026 (knee) · The BMJ, 2026 (hip)
y9-10: The blood pressure benefit of wall sits may last with just one session a week
y9-11: A randomised controlled trial published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine included 100 adults with a systolic blood pressure of 120–140 mmHg who did not exercise regularly, with an average age of 37. For 4 weeks, participants did wall sits at home three times a week: 4 bouts per session, with 2 minutes of seated rest in between. For the next 4 weeks, they continued with three, two or one session a week, or stopped. At week 8, systolic blood pressure was 13.7 mmHg lower than at the start with three sessions a week, 7.0 mmHg lower with two and 6.6 mmHg lower with one; in those who stopped, blood pressure returned to a level no different from the control group.
y9-12: None of the participants had high blood pressure, and the maintenance phase lasted only 4 weeks; longer studies are needed. One or two sessions a week may be enough to maintain the fall in the short term, but the additional benefits in vascular resistance and heart rate variability were maintained only with three sessions a week. If you have high blood pressure or take blood pressure medication, talk to your doctor before starting.
y9-13: Sources: BMJ Group, 29 September 2026 · BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, 2026
